title: Woven bar
subtitle: Needle-woven bars with a raised centre ridge across hardanger openwork
excerpt: A woven bar is worked across the same exposed thread groups as a wrapped bar, but instead of winding around all threads together, the needle weaves between two groups in a figure-of-eight motion. This builds up a raised, plaited surface with a distinct central ridge.
sourceNotes: Standard hardanger needle-weaving technique; documented in Elsie Svennas, A Handbook of Hardanger Embroidery (1977) and in general counted-thread needlework references.

content.text: After threads are cut and withdrawn from a hardanger square, the remaining threads are divided into two equal groups. The working thread passes alternately over one group and under the other in a figure-of-eight, building a tightly woven bar with a raised ridge down the middle. Woven bars are slightly more textured than wrapped bars and are the standard choice when dove's eye fillings will also be added.

items.label: Thread
items.value: Perle cotton no 8 for bars; no 5 was used for kloster blocks

items.label: Fabric
items.value: 28-count evenweave linen or 22-count hardanger fabric, with kloster blocks complete and threads already cut and withdrawn

content.text: must be complete before any threads are cut. Cut and withdraw the threads running parallel to the block stitches. The threads that remain, running perpendicular to the blocks, form the bar. On 28-count linen, a typical bar contains 4 threads, which are split into two groups of 2.

Secure the working thread under the back of a kloster block and bring it up at the base of the first bar. Separate the threads into two equal groups: hold one group above and one below the needle path.

Pass the needle over the top group, then under the bottom group, then pull the working thread through. Next, pass over the bottom group and under the top group and pull through. This figure-of-eight motion is one complete weaving cycle. Keep each pass snug but not so tight that the bar threads bunch together.

Continue weaving from one end of the bar to the other. The working thread builds up between the two groups of threads, raising a central ridge. When you reach the far kloster block, run the needle under its stitches on the back to move to the next bar.

If the design includes dove's eye fillings, stop at the midpoint of each of the four surrounding bars to work the looped filling before finishing those bars. Finish all bars fully if no filling is planned.

items.symptom: The ridge is uneven or the two groups of threads drift apart
items.cause: The two groups were not kept evenly separated during weaving, or the tension varied
items.fix: After each pass, ease the groups back into position with the needle tip before tightening the stitch. Keep the same tension throughout.

items.symptom: The bar is too short and does not reach the far kloster block
items.cause: The weaving passes were packed too loosely, or too few passes were made
items.fix: Push each woven pass firmly toward the starting end before placing the next, so the weaving is dense from the start. The finished bar should fill the full gap.

items.symptom: The bar threads fray at the cut ends
items.cause: Threads were cut at an angle or without a sharp enough scissor tip
items.fix: Use pointed embroidery scissors and cut straight across, as close as possible to the base of the kloster block stitches.
